description: Table 3 is a single rendered table — no plot, micrograph or schematic — captioned "Mechanical properties of the investigated steels" and reporting tensile results for four Fe-35Mn-xAl-0.1C low-density steels. It has five columns: a first column headed "Test temperature" whose entries are in fact the alloy labels 4Al, 6Al, 8Al and 10Al, then "Yield strength, MPa", "Ultimate tensile strength, MPa", "Uniform elongation, %" and "Total elongation, %". Four data rows are given, every value with a ± standard deviation: 4Al — 239 (±7) MPa, 552 (±12) MPa, 38.5 (±2.0) %, 52.0 (±1.8) %; 6Al — 251 (±3) MPa, 589 (±18) MPa, 37.6 (±0.9) %, 51.6 (±1.5) %; 8Al — 455 (±10) MPa, 740 (±14) MPa, 31.0 (±1.3) %, 39.8 (±1.8) %; 10Al — 585 (±29) MPa, 613 (±41) MPa, 2.1 (±1.1) %, 4.6 (±1.6) %. The table shows yield strength rising monotonically with Al content from 4Al to 10Al while uniform and total elongation fall, the collapse in ductility being catastrophic only for 10Al. Note the first-column header does not match its alloy-label entries.

observations.observation: The figure contains no image or curve; it is a 5-column, 4-row numeric table of tensile properties for the steels 4Al, 6Al, 8Al and 10Al.
The first column is headed "Test temperature" yet its four entries are the alloy labels 4Al, 6Al, 8Al and 10Al — the printed header is inconsistent with its content.
4Al: yield strength 239 (±7) MPa and ultimate tensile strength 552 (±12) MPa.
6Al: yield strength 251 (±3) MPa and ultimate tensile strength 589 (±18) MPa.
8Al: yield strength 455 (±10) MPa and ultimate tensile strength 740 (±14) MPa.
10Al: yield strength 585 (±29) MPa and ultimate tensile strength 613 (±41) MPa, i.e. the highest yield strength but a lower UTS than 8Al.
Uniform elongation decreases across the series: 38.5 (±2.0) % for 4Al, 37.6 (±0.9) % for 6Al, 31.0 (±1.3) % for 8Al and 2.1 (±1.1) % for 10Al.
Total elongation decreases across the series: 52.0 (±1.8) % for 4Al, 51.6 (±1.5) % for 6Al, 39.8 (±1.8) % for 8Al and 4.6 (±1.6) % for 10Al.
The table shows that 8Al retains appreciable ductility (31.0 % uniform, 39.8 % total elongation) while 10Al is nearly brittle (2.1 % uniform, 4.6 % total elongation).
The caption states the table gives the mechanical properties of the investigated steels (tensile test results).
The citing text states that as Al content increases from 4 wt% to 8 wt%, yield and tensile strength increase while uniform elongation only decreases from 38 % to 31 %.
The citing text states that at 10 % Al the yield strength rises to 585 MPa but tensile elongation is only about 4.6 %, exhibiting brittle characteristics.
The citing text attributes the degradation in plasticity of the 10Al steel to coarsening of DO3 ordered domains and formation of 18R martensite.

The citing sentence describing the 4Al→8Al change ("increase from 239 MPa to 552 MPa–455 MPa and 740 MPa") is ambiguous; read against the table it corresponds to yield strength 239 → 455 MPa and ultimate tensile strength 552 → 740 MPa, so the cited numbers and the table can only be reconciled by that reading.

subfigures.description: The whole figure is one data table with columns 'Test temperature', 'Yield strength, MPa', 'Ultimate tensile strength, MPa', 'Uniform elongation, %' and 'Total elongation, %', and four rows labelled 4Al, 6Al, 8Al, 10Al. All 16 data cells are legible and print mean values with ± standard deviations; there are no graphical elements, error bars or images.
